newsitem.title: USA: FDA panel backs Allergan intra-ocular lens.
newsitem.headline: FDA panel backs Allergan intra-ocular lens.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel voted 10-1 on Thursday in favor of a new intra-ocular lens (IOL) made by Allergan Inc.
However, the committee spent more time discussing the drawbacks of the AMO Array multifocal lens than its benefits.

IOLs, with global sales of about $400 million, are used to replace eyeball lenses damaged by cataracts. The AMO is designed to allow far-sighted patients to go without glasses after surgery, but the panel was not convinced that the lens improved patients' near or intermediate vision.
The panel was in favor of a long list of warnings and instructions to be given to physicians and patients.
Of special concern to the panel was an apparent difficult of patients to see in low-light conditions, such as driving at night.

An Allergan driving simulation study confirmed this weakness and also showed significant differences in sign recognition in different light conditions between patients with the AMO and monofocal IOLs.

Panelist James McCulley of the Texas Southwestern Medical Center noted other AMO limitations, most noticeably the inability of the lenses to improve the short-term vision of patients with small pupils.
Other concerns included a "halo effect" experienced by a quarter of those in trials and no benefits at all if surgeons place the lens off-center, McCulley said.
Allergan said the majority of patients it surveyed said that despite some drawbacks they would have the surgery again.

But panelist Gary Rubin of Johns Hopkins University said Allergan's figures were averages and could obscure problems. The firm conducted nearly a dozen studies with 400 patients in total, comparing monofocal IOLs to the AMO.
Allergan said these studies found that the AMO increased depth of focus and reduced patients' dependence on glasses such that 98 percent of patients achieved 20/40 or better nearsighted vision.
"That's pretty remarkable," said McCulley, noting that he still had reservations.
The need for IOLs was expected to grow as the population ages, but declining Medicare reimbursement may keep revenues flat to declining.
Theta Research of Rocky Hill, Conn. projected that IOL sales will drop to $208 million by 2000 from $270 million in 1995.
